mainTopic: כופר and intent, how an ox becomes מועד for killing, and the ban on eating or benefiting from an ox sentenced to death
overview: The amud opens by finishing אביי's and רבא's explanations of why there is no כופר when an ox killed a woman through רביעה. Their practical difference is an ox that tramples a child in the victim's yard. A ברייתא then supports רב: a stadium ox that kills is not put to death and stays fit for the מזבח, because it was forced. A new משנה teaches that only a מועד ox's owner pays כופר, that both a תם and a מועד ox are put to death, and that killing a slave costs a fixed thirty סלעים. The גמרא asks how an ox could ever become מועד for killing if it is put to death after its first killing. Many אמוראים answer: a court assessment, deadly wounds where the victims died later, an ox that ran to the marsh, witnesses who were disqualified and then restored, and an ox that could not be identified. Several answers are rejected along the way. Next, a ברייתא learns that an ox sentenced to death is forbidden to eat even if it was slaughtered first, and that the owner may get no benefit from it ('ובעל השור נקי'). The גמרא tests this against רבי אבהו's rule that 'do not eat' also means 'do not benefit.' מר זוטרא then begins a challenge that continues on the next amud.

steps.title: End of אביי's answer: the ox is not treated as the killer
steps.stepSummary: אביי finishes his explanation. Since the woman was put to death by בית דין, the ברייתא is teaching that the ox does not count as the one that killed her.
steps.simpleTranslation: [You might have thought] the ox is considered as if it killed her. The ברייתא comes to teach us [that it is not].
steps.whatsHappening: This line finishes אביי's answer from the end of the previous section. He explains why the ברייתא needed to say there is no כופר: it rules out the idea that the ox counts as her killer.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In אביי's reading, the ox only did רביעה, and the woman was then executed by בית דין for taking part. One could think the ox caused her death and so its owner should pay כופר. The ברייתא tells us no: the court's execution is not counted as the ox killing her.

keyTerms.meaning: It is as if it killed her
It teaches us (so we would not make that mistake)
Ransom payment an owner makes when his ox kills a person

steps.confusionAlert: This line opens partway through a sentence. The words 'you might have thought' (מהו דתימא) come right before it, in the previous section. So the ברייתא is rejecting the idea in this line, not agreeing with it.

phrases.english: it is like one that killed her,
it teaches us [that it is not so].

steps.triggerLanguage: כְּמַאן דְּקַטְלַהּ דָּמֵי, קָא מַשְׁמַע לַן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Finishes אביי's answer to the earlier question about why the ברייתא exempts the owner from כופר.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Redefining the case: the woman was executed by בית דין, so the ox was not the direct killer.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Because the ox caused her execution, it might count as if it killed her, and the owner would owe כופר.
steps.terutzMaskana: Being executed by the court does not count as being killed by the ox, so no כופר is paid.

steps.title: רבא: the ox did kill her, but it had no intent to harm
steps.stepSummary: רבא says the ox really killed her during the רביעה. There is still no כופר, because a goring horn means to harm, while here the ox only wanted its own pleasure.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבא said: Really, the case is where the ox did רביעה with her and killed her. And as for your question, 'What difference does it make whether it killed her with its horns or killed her through רביעה?' The answer is that a horn's goal is to cause harm, but this ox's goal was its own pleasure.
steps.whatsHappening: רבא gives a different explanation of the same ברייתא. He keeps the plain reading that the ox killed her, and explains why the owner still does not pay כופר.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Before this, the question was: if the ox killed her, why is this different from goring? רבא answers that כופר applies when the animal acts in a harmful way, like קרן. An ox that kills while chasing its own pleasure is a different kind of act, so there is no כופר.

keyTerms.meaning: Really / in fact (keeping the first reading)
Bestiality, an animal mating with a person
Horn; the category of damage done on purpose, like goring
Its intention is to cause damage
Its own pleasure

steps.whyThisMatters: This sets up the key question that separates אביי from רבא: is כופר paid only when the animal meant to harm?

phrases.english: Rava said:
Actually, it is where it engaged in bestiality with her and killed her;
and as for what is difficult for you:
what difference is it to me if it killed her with its horns,
what difference is it to me if it killed her through bestiality —
with a horn, its intention is to cause harm,
this one, its intention is for its own pleasure.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Offers a different answer from אביי's for the same ברייתא.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Making a distinction: כופר depends on whether the animal intended to harm.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Killing through רביעה seems no different from killing with the horns.
steps.terutzMaskana: Killing for the animal's own pleasure is not like goring, so there is no כופר.

steps.title: Where would אביי and רבא actually rule differently?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks what practical case would show the difference between the two explanations.
steps.simpleTranslation: In what case do they disagree?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא is setting up its next move. It asks for a real case where אביי's and רבא's approaches would give different rulings.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Both explanations agree that the ברייתא's owner pays no כופר. So the גמרא wants to know where the reasoning behind them would actually make a difference.

keyTerms.meaning: In what do they disagree? (asking for the practical difference)

phrases.english: In what do they disagree?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Compares the two explanations from steps 1 and 2.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: A case where אביי and רבא would rule differently.

steps.title: An ox that tramples a child in the victim's yard
steps.stepSummary: If an ox steps on a child and kills it in the victim's yard, אביי says the owner pays כופר and רבא says he does not.
steps.simpleTranslation: They disagree about a foot (רגל) that stepped on a child in the victim's yard. According to אביי, the owner pays כופר. According to רבא, he does not pay כופר.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers its question with a case where the ox killed but did not mean to cause harm.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Stepping (רגל) is ordinary walking, not an attempt to harm. For אביי, כופר does not need intent to harm, so the owner pays. For רבא, כופר needs intent to harm, like קרן, so the owner does not pay.

keyTerms.meaning: Foot; damage an animal does just by walking normally
Trampled / stepped on
The yard of the person who was harmed
A small child

steps.whatToRemember: אביי says כופר is paid even without intent to harm. רבא says כופר is paid only when the animal meant to harm. Their test case is רגל trampling a child in the victim's yard.

phrases.english: about a foot that trampled on a child
in the yard of the injured party;
according to Abaye — he pays ransom,
according to Rava — he does not pay ransom.

steps.triggerLanguage: בְּרֶגֶל שֶׁדָּרְסָה עַל גַּבֵּי תִּינוֹק בַּחֲצַר הַנִּיזָּק
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question in step 3.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The case of רגל trampling a child in the victim's yard: אביי requires כופר and רבא does not.

steps.title: A ברייתא supports רב about the stadium ox
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא teaches that a stadium ox that kills is not put to death and may still be brought on the מזבח, because it was forced into acting that way. This supports רב.
steps.simpleTranslation: A ברייתא is taught in line with רב: A stadium ox is not put to death, and it is fit for the מזבח, because it is as if it was forced.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a ברייתא that supports an earlier statement of רב about an ox trained to fight in an arena.
steps.deeperAnalysis: An ox that kills is normally stoned, and it may not be used as a קרבן. But a stadium ox was provoked and trained by people to fight. So it is treated as if it was forced, and neither rule applies to it.

keyTerms.meaning: A ברייתא is taught that agrees with him
A stadium ox, trained to fight in an arena
Must be put to death
Fit to be offered on the altar
As if forced / compelled

steps.whatToRemember: An animal pushed into violence by people is treated as forced. It is not put to death, and it stays fit for the מזבח.

phrases.english: It is taught in accordance with Rav:
a stadium ox — is not liable to death,
and it is fit for the altar;
because it is as though compelled.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Leaves the אביי and רבא discussion and brings support for an earlier ruling of רב.
steps.raayaObject: רב's ruling about the stadium ox.
steps.raayaSupportSource: A ברייתא: a stadium ox is not put to death and is fit for the מזבח, because it is as if forced.

steps.title: An ox that kills a person: ransom and death
steps.stepSummary: The משנה rules that only the owner of a מועד ox pays כופר. Both a תם and a מועד ox are put to death, and the same law applies to a boy or a girl.
steps.simpleTranslation: משנה: If an ox gored a person and the person died, the owner of a מועד ox pays כופר, and the owner of a תם ox is exempt from כופר. Both kinds of ox are put to death. The same applies if the victim was a boy or a girl.
steps.whatsHappening: A new משנה begins. It lays out what happens when an ox kills a person.
steps.deeperAnalysis: There are two separate results here. The first is money: the owner pays כופר, and only for a מועד ox. The second is the ox's punishment: it is put to death whether it is תם or מועד. The rule is the same whether the victim was an adult, a boy, or a girl.

keyTerms.meaning: Short for מתניתין, 'our משנה'
A forewarned ox that has an established habit of goring
An innocuous ox with no record of goring
The ransom payment the owner pays when his ox kills a person
They are liable to be put to death

steps.confusionAlert: Do not mix up the two results. Being exempt from כופר does not save a תם ox from being put to death. The owner of a תם is only free from paying money.

phrases.english: MISHNAH:
An ox that gored a person, and the person died:
if it was forewarned, the owner pays ransom,
and if it was innocuous, he is exempt from the ransom.
And both this one and that one are liable to death.
And the same applies with a boy, and the same with a girl.
phrases.notes: This follows the פסוק in שמות 21:31.

steps.triggerLanguage: מַתְנִי׳ שׁוֹר שֶׁנָּגַח אֶת הָאָדָם, וּמֵת
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts a new משנה after the previous discussion of רבא, אביי, and the stadium ox.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Only a מועד's owner pays כופר. Both a תם and a מועד ox are put to death. The law is the same for a boy or a girl victim.

steps.title: An ox that kills a slave: a fixed thirty סלעים
steps.stepSummary: If the ox kills a slave or a maidservant, the owner pays a fixed thirty סלעים, no matter what the slave was worth.
steps.simpleTranslation: If it gored a slave or a maidservant, the owner gives thirty סלעים. This is true whether the slave was worth a hundred מנה or worth only one דינר.
steps.whatsHappening: The משנה continues with a different kind of victim, a slave. The payment for a slave is a set amount.
steps.deeperAnalysis: For a free person, the payment is כופר. For a slave, the Torah sets a fixed fine of thirty סלעים. The slave's actual market value, whether very high or very low, makes no difference.

keyTerms.meaning: A slave or a maidservant
Thirty סלעים, the fixed payment set by the Torah
A large sum worth one hundred דינרים
A small coin

steps.whatToRemember: An ox that kills is put to death whether it is תם or מועד. Only a מועד's owner pays כופר. For a slave, the payment is always exactly thirty סלעים.

phrases.english: If it gored a slave or a maidservant,
he gives thirty selaim,
whether he is worth a hundred maneh,

phrases.aramaic: וּבֵין שֶׁאֵינוֹ יָפֶה אֶלָּא דִּינָר אֶחָד.
phrases.english: or whether he is worth only one dinar.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the משנה with the case of a slave victim.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: For killing a slave, the owner pays a fixed thirty סלעים, regardless of the slave's value.

steps.title: How can there ever be a forewarned ox for killing?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks a problem. A תם ox is put to death after its first killing, so how could an ox ever become מועד for killing people?
steps.simpleTranslation: גמרא: But since we kill the ox already while it is תם, how can you ever find a מועד ox?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges the משנה's case of a מועד ox that pays כופר. It asks how such a case could ever happen.
steps.deeperAnalysis: An ox becomes מועד by goring three times. But once an ox kills a person, it is put to death right away, even while it is still תם. So it seems an ox could never reach three killings, and the משנה's case of a מועד that kills looks impossible.

keyTerms.meaning: Short for גמרא
We kill it already while it is תם
How can you find such a case?

phrases.english: GEMARA:
But since we kill it already while it is innocuous,
how can you find a forewarned one?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Attacks the משנה's case of a מועד ox that kills.
steps.kashyaTarget: The משנה's ruling that a מועד ox that kills makes its owner pay כופר.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Becoming מועד takes three gorings, but a killer ox is put to death after its first killing. So a מועד for killing seems impossible.

steps.title: רבה: the court assessed it would have killed three people
steps.stepSummary: רבה answers that the ox attacked three people, and the court judged that it would have killed each of them. That makes it מועד even though no one actually died.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבה said: Here we are dealing with a case where the court assessed it regarding three people, judging that it would have killed them.
steps.whatsHappening: רבה answers the question. He describes a case where an ox can become מועד without having killed anyone yet.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The ox attacked three people, and the court judged that it would certainly have killed them had they not escaped. Since no one died, the ox was never put to death. But the court's judgment counts as three killing attacks, so the ox becomes מועד.

keyTerms.meaning: With what case are we dealing here?
They assessed it; the court judged what the ox would have done

phrases.english: Rabba said:
With what are we dealing here?
For example, where they assessed it regarding three people.
phrases.notes: The court judged that the ox would surely have killed them if they had not escaped.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of step 8.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Defines a specific case in which the משנה works.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: A מועד for killing seemed impossible.
steps.terutzMaskana: The court's judgment that the ox would have killed three people makes it מועד without any actual death.

steps.title: רב אשי: an assessment is worth nothing
steps.stepSummary: רב אשי rejects רבה's answer. He says the court's guess about what the ox would have done means nothing.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב אשי said: An assessment is not anything.
steps.whatsHappening: רב אשי pushes back on רבה. He refuses to let a mere assessment make an ox מועד.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In רב אשי's view, what the ox might have done does not count. Only what it actually did matters. So רבה's case does not create a מועד, and a new answer is needed.

keyTerms.meaning: An assessment or estimate
It is nothing; it has no legal weight

phrases.english: Rav Ashi said:
An assessment is not anything.

steps.triggerLanguage: רַב אָשֵׁי אָמַר: אוּמְדָּנָא לָאו כְּלוּם הוּא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Rejects רבה's answer in step 9.
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: רבה's whole answer, which was based on the court's assessment.
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: An assessment of what the ox would have done has no legal weight. Only actual harm counts.

steps.title: רב אשי: it fatally wounded three people who died later
steps.stepSummary: רב אשי gives his own answer. The ox fatally wounded three people, and they all died only after the third goring, so the ox was never put to death before becoming מועד.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, here we are dealing with a case where it endangered three people.
steps.whatsHappening: After rejecting רבה, רב אשי offers his own case that explains how a מועד for killing can exist.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The ox gored three people, and each was badly wounded. None of them died until after the third goring. Since there was no death yet, the ox was not put to death in the meantime. Here the gorings are real harm, not a guess, so the ox is truly מועד.

keyTerms.meaning: It endangered; it wounded them so badly that their lives were at risk

steps.whatToRemember: The question is how an ox can become מועד for killing. רבה answers with the court's assessment. רב אשי rejects assessments and answers instead with real deadly wounds where the deaths came only later.

phrases.english: Rather, with what are we dealing here?
For example, where it endangered three people.
phrases.notes: It wounded all three badly, and they died only after the third goring, so the ox wasn't put to death first.

steps.triggerLanguage: אֶלָּא הָכָא בְּמַאי עָסְקִינַן – כְּגוֹן שֶׁסִּיכֵּן לִשְׁלֹשָׁה בְּנֵי אָדָם
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives רב אשי's replacement answer after rejecting רבה in step 10.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Gives a different case definition that is based on actual harm.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: רבה relied on an assessment of what the ox would have done.
steps.terutzMaskana: Three real deadly gorings, with the deaths coming only after the third, make the ox מועד before it is ever put to death.

steps.title: The ox killed three animals
steps.stepSummary: רב זביד suggests that the ox became מועד by killing three animals, which does not get an ox put to death.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב זביד said: It is talking about an ox that killed three animals.
steps.whatsHappening: רב זביד offers a new answer to the question from Step 8. He says the ox became מועד by killing three animals.
steps.deeperAnalysis: An ox is not put to death for killing an animal, so it stays alive after each killing. That way it can build up three killings and become מועד. רב זביד is trying to find a path that avoids the death penalty problem.

keyTerms.meaning: For example, such as. It introduces the case being suggested.
Animals.
That it killed.

phrases.english: Rav Zevid said:
For example, where it killed three animals.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives another answer to the question of Step 8, next to רב אשי's answer.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Redefines the case so the earlier killings did not carry a death penalty.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: No ox could ever become מועד for killing, because it would be put to death after the first killing.
steps.terutzMaskana: The ox killed three animals, so it was never put to death and could become מועד.

steps.title: Killing animals does not make it dangerous to people
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא rejects רב זביד: being מועד for animals does not make an ox מועד for people.
steps.simpleTranslation: But is an ox that is מועד for animals considered מועד for people?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא pushes back on רב זביד. An ox known to kill animals is not automatically known to kill people.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Being מועד is about a specific habit. An ox that goes after animals has shown a habit with animals, not with humans. So three animal killings cannot make it מועד for killing a person.

keyTerms.meaning: An ox with a proven habit of harming, after doing it three times.
Is it considered? Here it asks a pointed question.
For people.

phrases.english: But one that is forewarned for animals,
is it forewarned for people?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Rejects רב זביד's answer from Step 12.
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: Being מועד for one kind of victim (animals) does not carry over to another kind (people).

steps.title: The ox killed three גוים
steps.stepSummary: רב שימי suggests the ox killed three גוים, which does not get the ox put to death.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, רב שימי said: It is talking about an ox that killed three גוים.
steps.whatsHappening: Since the animal case failed, רב שימי offers a case where the victims were people. He says the ox killed three גוים.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This time the victims are human, which fixes the problem from Step 13. But an ox is not put to death for killing a גוי, so it can stay alive to reach three killings.

keyTerms.meaning: Rather. It shows the earlier answer was dropped and a new one is coming.
Non-Jews.

phrases.english: Rather, Rav Shimi said:
For example, where it killed three gentiles.
phrases.notes: The ox is not put to death for these killings, so it stays alive.

steps.triggerLanguage: אֶלָּא אָמַר רַב שִׁימִי: כְּגוֹן שֶׁהָרַג שְׁלֹשָׁה גּוֹיִם
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Replaces רב זביד's rejected answer with a case where the victims are human.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Redefines the case so the victims were people, but the killings still carried no death penalty.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Animal killings do not count, so there is still no way for an ox to become מועד for people.
steps.terutzMaskana: The ox killed three גוים, so it was never put to death and could become מועד for people.

steps.title: Killing גוים does not make it מועד for Jews
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא rejects רב שימי: being מועד for גוים does not make the ox מועד for Jews.
steps.simpleTranslation: But is an ox that is מועד for גוים considered מועד for Jews?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא pushes back on רב שימי with the same kind of question as before.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The גמרא treats killing גוים and killing Jews as different categories here. So an ox with a habit for one is not proven to have a habit for the other. The same reasoning as Step 13 knocks down this answer too.

keyTerms.meaning: Forewarned with regard to non-Jews.
Jews.
Forewarned with regard to Jews.

phrases.english: But one that is forewarned for gentiles,
is it forewarned for Jews?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Rejects רב שימי's answer using the same pattern as Step 13.
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: Being מועד for one category of victim does not carry over to a different category.

steps.title: The ox killed three people who were טרפה
steps.stepSummary: ריש לקיש suggests the ox killed three Jews who were טרפה, already fatally ill or injured.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, רבי שמעון בן לקיש said: It is talking about an ox that killed three people who were טרפה.
steps.whatsHappening: ריש לקיש offers a case where the victims were Jewish people, but people who were already going to die. He says the ox killed three people who were טרפה.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A טרפה person has a fatal injury and would die anyway. The ox is not put to death for killing such a person, so it can stay alive and reach three killings. This fixes the problem of Step 15, since the victims are now Jews.

keyTerms.meaning: A person with a fatal injury who will not live long.
People, human beings.

phrases.aramaic: אֶלָּא אָמַר רַבִּי שִׁמְעוֹן בֶּן לָקִישׁ:
phrases.english: Rather, Rabbi Shimon ben Lakish said:

phrases.aramaic: כְּגוֹן שֶׁהָרַג שְׁלֹשָׁה בְּנֵי אָדָם טְרֵפָה.
phrases.english: For example, where it killed three people who were tereifa.
phrases.notes: These people were going to die anyway, so the ox is not put to death for killing them.

steps.triggerLanguage: אֶלָּא אָמַר רַבִּי שִׁמְעוֹן בֶּן לָקִישׁ: כְּגוֹן שֶׁהָרַג שְׁלֹשָׁה בְּנֵי אָדָם טְרֵפָה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Replaces רב שימי's rejected answer with a case of Jewish victims who were טרפה.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Redefines the victims as people whose killing carries no death penalty for the ox.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Killings of גוים do not count for Jews, so there is still no way to become מועד.
steps.terutzMaskana: The ox killed three טרפה people, so it was not put to death and could become מועד.

steps.title: Killing טרפה people does not make it מועד for healthy people
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא rejects ריש לקיש: being מועד for טרפה people does not make the ox מועד for healthy people.
steps.simpleTranslation: But is an ox that is מועד for a טרפה considered מועד for a healthy person?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא pushes back on ריש לקיש with the same kind of question a third time.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A טרפה person is weak and close to death, so killing one may be easier. An ox that killed weak people has not proven it will kill healthy, whole people. So this answer fails too.

keyTerms.meaning: Whole, healthy. A person who is not טרפה.
Forewarned with regard to a טרפה person.
Forewarned with regard to a healthy person.

phrases.english: But one that is forewarned for a tereifa,
is it forewarned for an intact person?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Rejects ריש לקיש's answer using the same pattern as Steps 13 and 15.
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: Killing weak, dying people does not prove a habit of killing healthy people.

steps.title: The ox killed and ran away to the marsh each time
steps.stepSummary: רב פפא says the ox killed and ran away to the marsh each time, so the court could not catch it until it had killed three times.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, רב פפא said: It killed and ran away to the marsh, and killed again and ran away to the marsh.
steps.whatsHappening: רב פפא gives a simple, practical answer. The ox did deserve to be put to death, but it kept escaping before the court could catch it.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Unlike the earlier answers, the victims here are regular, healthy Jewish people, so the problem of a different category is gone. The ox stayed alive only because it ran off to the marsh each time. By the time it was caught, it had killed three times and was מועד.

keyTerms.meaning: That it killed.
And it ran away.
A marsh, a swampy area where an animal could hide.

steps.whatToRemember: The גמרא rejected three answers (animals, גוים, טרפה people) because a habit with one kind of victim does not prove a habit with another kind. רב פפא's answer works because the ox killed regular people three times and simply kept escaping.

phrases.english: Rather, Rav Pappa said:
Where it killed and fled to the marsh,
killed and fled to the marsh.

steps.triggerLanguage: אֶלָּא אָמַר רַב פָּפָּא: דִּקְטַל וַעֲרַק לְאַגְמָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Replaces ריש לקיש's rejected answer with a case that avoids all the earlier problems.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Practical case: the ox deserved death but escaped before the court could act.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Every case of three killings either gets the ox put to death or involves a different kind of victim.
steps.terutzMaskana: The ox killed healthy people three times and escaped each time, so it became מועד for people.

steps.title: The witnesses who disqualified the testimony were themselves disqualified
steps.stepSummary: רב אחא בריה דרב איקא says the ox was not killed because the witnesses against it were made זוממין. Later, those who made them זוממין were themselves made זוממין, so the original testimony about all three killings came back.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב אחא, son of רב איקא, said: The case is where the witnesses who proved the first witnesses to be זוממין were themselves proven זוממין.
steps.whatsHappening: Another אמורא gives a new answer to how an ox could kill three times without being put to death.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Each time the ox killed, witnesses testified, but a second pair proved them זוממין, so the court did not kill the ox. Later, a third pair proved the second pair זוממין. That brought back the first testimony about all three killings at once, so the ox is now a מועד.

keyTerms.meaning: were proven to be lying witnesses through הזמה (other witnesses showed they were somewhere else at the time)
the witnesses who caught other witnesses as זוממין, who are then caught themselves
plotting witnesses whose testimony is thrown out by הזמה

steps.confusionAlert: There are three sets of witnesses here. The first set saw the killing. The second set disqualified the first. The third set disqualified the second, and that brings the first set's testimony back to life.

phrases.aramaic: רַב אַחָא בְּרֵיהּ דְּרַב אִיקָא אָמַר:
phrases.english: Rav Aḥa, son of Rav Ika, said:
Such as where the witnesses who had rendered the others conspirators were themselves rendered conspirators.
phrases.notes: Once the middle witnesses are knocked out, the first witnesses' story about the ox counts again.

steps.triggerLanguage: רַב אַחָא בְּרֵיהּ דְּרַב אִיקָא אָמַר: כְּגוֹן שֶׁהוּזְמוּ זוֹמְמֵי זוֹמְמִין
steps.relationToPreviousStep: A new, separate answer to the same question that רב פפא answered.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Case limitation: the testimony was thrown out and then brought back.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: It seems an ox could never kill three times, because the court would kill it after the first time.
steps.terutzMaskana: The court never killed it because the testimony was thrown out. When that testimony came back, all three killings were proven at once.

steps.title: But then the owner was never warned
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא says this answer works if becoming a מועד is about proving something about the ox. But if it is about warning the owner, he can say he did not know, since the testimony had been thrown out.
steps.simpleTranslation: This works well if we need to make the ox a מועד. But if we need to warn the man, he can say: I didn't know!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges רב אחא's answer from the side of the owner.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If being a מועד means the ox is shown to be a killer, bringing back the testimony is enough. But if the point is to warn the owner, he has a good excuse. When the killings happened, the testimony had been canceled, so he had no reason to think his ox was dangerous.

keyTerms.meaning: this works well (used to open a challenge: it works one way, but not the other)
to make מועד; to establish as warned
the man, here the owner of the ox

phrases.aramaic: הָנִיחָא אִי לְיַיעוֹדֵי תּוֹרָא בָּעֵינַן – שַׁפִּיר.
phrases.english: This works out if we need to make the ox forewarned, it is fine.
But if we need to warn the man,

phrases.aramaic: מֵימַר אֲמַר לֵיהּ: לָא הֲוָה יָדַעְנָא!
phrases.english: he can say to him: I did not know!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges רב אחא's answer.
steps.kashyaTarget: רב אחא בריה דרב איקא's case of זוממי זוממין
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: If becoming a מועד requires warning the owner, an owner whose witnesses were thrown out was never really warned.

steps.title: The owner was standing right there each time
steps.stepSummary: The witnesses say that every time the ox killed, the owner was standing next to it. So he cannot claim he did not know.
steps.simpleTranslation: The case is where the witnesses say: Each time his ox killed, he was standing next to it.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא defends רב אחא's answer by adding a detail to the case.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The owner saw every killing with his own eyes. Whether or not the court accepted the testimony, he knew what his ox did, so he was truly warned.

keyTerms.meaning: every time
he was standing next to it

phrases.aramaic: כְּגוֹן דְּאָמְרִי: כֹּל אֵימַת דְּקָטֵיל תּוֹרֵיהּ,
phrases.english: Such as where they say: Every time that his ox killed,
he was standing next to it.

steps.triggerLanguage: כְּגוֹן דְּאָמְרִי: כֹּל אֵימַת דְּקָטֵיל תּוֹרֵיהּ גַּבֵּיהּ הֲוָה קָאֵי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge in step 20.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Adds a detail to the case.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The owner could claim he was never warned.
steps.terutzMaskana: He saw each killing himself, so he cannot claim he did not know.

steps.title: They knew the owner but not which ox
steps.stepSummary: רבינא says the witnesses recognized whose ox it was but could not identify the ox itself. So the court could not kill it, until later it was identified as the one that killed three times.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבינא said: The case is where they recognize the owner of the ox but do not recognize the ox.
steps.whatsHappening: רבינא gives yet another answer to how an ox could kill three times without being put to death.
steps.deeperAnalysis: To put an ox to death, the court must know exactly which ox did it. Here the witnesses only knew it belonged to this owner, so no ox could be put to death. Later it became clear that one particular ox was behind all three killings.

keyTerms.meaning: recognize, can identify
the owner of the ox

phrases.english: Ravina said:
Where they recognize the owner of the ox,
but they do not recognize the ox.

steps.triggerLanguage: רָבִינָא אָמַר: בְּמַכִּירִין אֶת בַּעַל הַשּׁוֹר וְאֵין מַכִּירִין אֶת הַשּׁוֹר
steps.relationToPreviousStep: A new, separate answer to the same question.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Case limitation: the ox could not be identified.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: An ox would always be put to death after its first killing.
steps.terutzMaskana: Without knowing which ox it was, the court could not put it to death, so it could kill three times.

steps.title: What could the owner have done?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks: if the owner did not know which of his oxen was the killer, why should he be treated as warned? What could he have done?
steps.simpleTranslation: What could he have done?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges רבינא's answer: it seems unfair to treat the owner as warned.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The point of a מועד is that the owner was warned and should have guarded his ox. But if nobody knew which ox it was, the owner did not know which one to guard.

keyTerms.meaning: what should he have done?

phrases.english: What could he have done?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges רבינא's answer.
steps.kashyaTarget: רבינא's case where the ox was not identified
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: An owner who could not know which ox was dangerous does not seem to have been warned.

steps.title: He should have guarded his whole herd
steps.stepSummary: The owner was told he has a goring ox somewhere in his herd. So he had to guard all his oxen.
steps.simpleTranslation: Because they say to him: You have a goring ox in your herd; you should have guarded your entire herd.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא defends רבינא's answer: the owner had something he could have done.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Even without knowing which ox it was, the owner knew one of his oxen kills. That knowledge alone required him to guard every ox, so he counts as warned.

keyTerms.meaning: a goring ox, one in the habit of goring
your herd of cattle
to guard

steps.whatToRemember: Here the גמרא gives two more cases where an ox kills three times without being put to death. In רב אחא's case, the testimony was canceled and later restored, and the owner saw the killings himself. In רבינא's case, the ox could not be identified, and the owner had to guard his whole herd.

phrases.english: Because they say to him:
You have a goring ox in your herd,
you should have guarded your entire herd.

steps.triggerLanguage: מִשּׁוּם דְּאָמְרִי לֵיהּ: תּוֹרָא נַגְחָנָא אִית לָךְ בְּבַקְרָךְ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge in step 23.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Widens the owner's duty to guard.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Since the owner could not know which ox was dangerous, he should not count as warned.
steps.terutzMaskana: Knowing one of his oxen gores required him to guard the whole herd, so he counts as warned.

steps.title: Quoting the משנה: both oxen are put to death
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא quotes the next line of the משנה: both the מועד and the תם that killed a person are put to death.
steps.simpleTranslation: The משנה says: both this ox and that ox are liable to death, and so on.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא opens a new topic by quoting a line from the משנה. This sets up the ברייתא that comes next.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Up to now the discussion was about how an ox becomes a מועד. Now the focus shifts to what happens to the ox itself after it kills. Whether it was a תם or a מועד, it is put to death.

keyTerms.meaning: Both this one and that one (the תם and the מועד)
Are liable to be put to death
Etc.: the rest of the משנה's line

phrases.english: And both this one and that one are liable to death, etc.
phrases.notes: 'This one and that one' means the מועד ox and the תם ox from the משנה.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts a new section, moving from the מועד discussion to the ox's death and its meat.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Any ox that kills a person, תם or מועד, is put to death.

steps.title: The ox is forbidden to eat even if slaughtered after the verdict
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא says the words 'לא יאכל את בשרו' would be extra if they only meant a stoned carcass. So they teach that even an ox slaughtered after its verdict may not be eaten.
steps.simpleTranslation: The Rabbis taught: the פסוק says 'the ox shall be stoned.' Don't I already know from that that it is a נבילה, and a נבילה may not be eaten? So why does the פסוק add 'its flesh shall not be eaten'? It is telling you that if someone slaughtered the ox after its verdict was given, it is still forbidden to eat.
steps.whatsHappening: A ברייתא notices that part of the פסוק seems extra and uses it to teach a new rule.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A stoned animal is a נבילה, which is already forbidden to eat. So 'לא יאכל את בשרו' must be teaching something new: an ox that was properly slaughtered after its sentence is still forbidden. Once the verdict is final, the ox is already forbidden, even though it was never stoned.

keyTerms.meaning: An animal that died without proper שחיטה; forbidden to eat
Why does the פסוק need to say this? (points out extra words)
Its verdict was finished; the court gave its final ruling
He slaughtered it properly

steps.whyThisMatters: This sets up a key rule: once the court has sentenced the ox, it is forbidden, even if it is never stoned.

phrases.english: The Rabbis taught:
From what is implied by what is said,
"The ox shall surely be stoned"
don't I know that it is a carcass,
and a carcass is forbidden to eat?
So why does the verse say
"its flesh shall not be eaten"?
The verse is telling you
that if he slaughtered it
after its verdict was given,
it is forbidden to eat.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Brings a ברייתא about the ox that the משנה just said is put to death.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: An ox slaughtered after its death verdict is forbidden to eat, learned from the extra words 'לא יאכל את בשרו'.

steps.title: What about benefit from the ox?
steps.stepSummary: The ברייתא asks: we know the ox can't be eaten, but where do we learn that you can't get any benefit from it either?
steps.simpleTranslation: So far I only know that it is forbidden to eat. Where do we learn that it is forbidden to get benefit from it?
steps.whatsHappening: The ברייתא asks a follow-up question, preparing for the source that comes next.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A ban on eating does not by itself mean a ban on all benefit, such as selling the ox or using its hide. The ברייתא wants a separate source for that stricter rule.

keyTerms.meaning: I only know (this much so far)
Benefit: any use or profit from something
From where do we learn it?

phrases.english: I only know about eating;
where do we learn about benefit?

steps.triggerLanguage: אֵין לִי אֶלָּא בַּאֲכִילָה, בַּהֲנָאָה מִנַּיִן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Extends the eating rule and asks about a ban on benefit.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: A source that the ox is forbidden for benefit, not only for eating.

steps.title: The source for the benefit ban: 'ובעל השור נקי'
steps.stepSummary: The ברייתא answers that the ban on benefit comes from 'and the owner of the ox shall be clear.'
steps.simpleTranslation: The פסוק says: 'And the owner of the ox shall be clear.'
steps.whatsHappening: The ברייתא answers its question with the last words of the same פסוק.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The words 'ובעל השור נקי' are read as saying the owner ends up 'clean' of the ox, with nothing left from it. How these words show this is explained in the next steps.

keyTerms.meaning: The פסוק teaches by saying
The owner of the ox
Clear / clean

phrases.english: The verse says:
"And the owner of the ox shall be clear."

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of step 27.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The benefit ban comes from 'ובעל השור נקי'.

steps.title: How do those words show a ban on benefit?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks how 'the owner shall be clear' teaches that benefit is forbidden.
steps.simpleTranslation: What does it imply?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks how the words of the פסוק lead to this rule, and sets up שמעון בן זומא's explanation.
steps.deeperAnalysis: 'The owner shall be clear' could simply mean he does not pay for the death. The גמרא wants to know how it can mean he may not benefit from the ox.

keyTerms.meaning: What does it imply? How do the words show this?

phrases.english: What is the implication?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Asks for the reasoning behind the source in step 28.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: How the word 'נקי' teaches a ban on benefit.

steps.title: שמעון בן זומא: 'clear' like a man left with nothing
steps.stepSummary: שמעון בן זומא explains that 'נקי' is used the way people say someone 'came out clean of his property': he has nothing left from it.
steps.simpleTranslation: שמעון בן זומא says: it is like a person who tells his friend, 'So-and-so came out clean of his property, and he has no benefit at all from it.'
steps.whatsHappening: שמעון בן זומא answers by pointing to how people use the word 'clean' in everyday speech.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In normal speech, being 'clean' of your property means you have lost it completely and get nothing from it. So 'the owner of the ox shall be clear' means the owner is cut off from the ox and may get no benefit from it.

keyTerms.meaning: So-and-so
His property
At all; of anything

steps.whatToRemember: An ox sentenced to death is forbidden to eat, even if slaughtered after the verdict ('לא יאכל את בשרו'). It is also forbidden for benefit ('ובעל השור נקי': the owner is left 'clean' of it).

phrases.english: Shimon ben Zoma says:
It is like a person who says to his friend:
"So-and-so came out clean of his property,

phrases.aramaic: וְאֵין לוֹ בָּהֶם הֲנָאָה שֶׁל כְּלוּם״.
phrases.english: and he has no benefit from it at all."

steps.triggerLanguage: שִׁמְעוֹן בֶּן זוֹמָא אוֹמֵר, כְּאָדָם שֶׁאוֹמֵר לַחֲבֵירוֹ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers step 29's question about the word 'נקי'.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: 'נקי' means left with nothing from the ox, the way people speak of someone cleaned out of his property.

steps.title: Maybe 'its flesh shall not be eaten' is about a stoned ox
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא challenges the ברייתא: why read 'לא יאכל את בשרו' as being about a slaughtered ox? Maybe a slaughtered ox is allowed, and these words are about a stoned ox and forbid benefit, like רבי אבהו says.
steps.simpleTranslation: And how do we know that 'its flesh shall not be eaten' is about a case where he slaughtered it after the verdict, making it forbidden to eat? Maybe if he slaughtered it after the verdict, it is allowed to eat. And 'its flesh shall not be eaten' is about a case where they actually stoned it, teaching that it is forbidden for benefit, like רבי אבהו.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא pushes back on the ברייתא of step 26 and offers a different way to read the same words.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The ברייתא said the words are extra, so they must be about a slaughtered ox. The גמרא answers that they could still be about a stoned ox. They would not be repeating the eating ban but adding a ban on benefit, following רבי אבהו. If so, nothing would forbid eating an ox slaughtered after its verdict.

keyTerms.meaning: And from where do we know? (opens a challenge)
Say instead: offers another possibility
Permitted
They actually stoned it

steps.confusionAlert: This challenge does not say the ox may be benefited from. It only questions which case 'לא יאכל את בשרו' is talking about: a slaughtered ox or a stoned one.

phrases.english: And from where do we know that "its flesh shall not be eaten"
is about a case where he slaughtered it
after its verdict was given,
teaching that it is forbidden to eat?
Say instead that where he slaughtered it
after its verdict was given,
it is permitted to eat;
and this "its flesh shall not be eaten"
is about a case where they actually stoned it,
teaching that it is forbidden for benefit,
in line with Rabbi Abbahu,

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Goes back to the ברייתא's reading in step 26 and challenges it.
steps.kashyaTarget: The ברייתא's claim that 'לא יאכל את בשרו' forbids eating an ox slaughtered after its verdict.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The words are not necessarily extra about eating. They could refer to a stoned ox and add a ban on benefit, following רבי אבהו. Then a slaughtered ox would be permitted to eat.

steps.title: רבי אבהו's rule: 'do not eat' also means 'do not benefit'
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא quotes the rule of רבי אבהו in the name of רבי אלעזר that it relied on in its challenge. Wherever the Torah says 'do not eat,' benefit is forbidden too, unless the Torah clearly says otherwise, as it does with נבילה.
steps.simpleTranslation: As רבי אבהו said in the name of רבי אלעזר: wherever the Torah says 'it shall not be eaten,' 'you shall not eat' (to one person), or 'you shall not eat' (to many people), both eating and benefit are forbidden. The only exception is when the Torah spells out that benefit is allowed, as it did with נבילה: you may give it to a גר and sell it to a non-Jew.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא is giving the source behind the challenge in step 31. It explains which rule of רבי אבהו it meant.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבי אבהו says that the words 'do not eat' normally cover benefit as well. So the challenge says 'לא יאכל את בשרו' by the ox could be the ban on benefit for a stoned ox. נבילה proves the rule: the Torah had to say outright that you may give or sell it, which shows that without those words, benefit would be forbidden.

keyTerms.meaning: A ban on eating something
A ban on getting any benefit or use from something
Is included in the meaning of the words
An animal that died without a kosher slaughter
Here, a non-Jew living in ארץ ישראל who keeps the seven מצוות of בני נח

steps.whyThisMatters: This rule of רבי אבהו is used all over ש״ס to decide when a food is also forbidden for benefit.

phrases.aramaic: דְּאָמַר רַבִּי אֲבָהוּ אָמַר רַבִּי אֶלְעָזָר:
phrases.english: As Rabbi Abbahu said in the name of Rabbi Elazar:
Any place where it says
"it shall not be eaten," "you shall not eat" (to one person), "you shall not eat" (to many people)
both a ban on eating
and a ban on benefit are meant,
unless the verse spells it out for you
the way it spelled it out for you with an animal carcass:
to a resident foreigner by giving it,
and to a non-Jew by selling it!

steps.triggerLanguage: דְּאָמַר רַבִּי אֲבָהוּ אָמַר רַבִּי אֶלְעָזָר
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives the source of the rule the challenge in step 31 depends on.
steps.raayaObject: The claim that 'לא יאכל את בשרו' could be a ban on benefit for a stoned ox.
steps.raayaSupportSource: רבי אבהו in the name of רבי אלעזר: 'do not eat' covers benefit too, as נבילה shows.

steps.title: The extra words 'its flesh' show the verse is about a slaughtered ox
steps.stepSummary: The answer: רבי אבהו's rule only applies when the eating ban itself comes from 'לא יאכל.' By the ox, the eating ban already comes from 'סקל יסקל,' and 'את בשרו' is extra. It teaches that even if the ox was slaughtered, it is forbidden.
steps.simpleTranslation: They answered: רבי אבהו's rule applies when both the eating ban and the benefit ban come from the words 'it shall not be eaten.' Here the eating ban already comes from 'it shall surely be stoned.' If 'its flesh shall not be eaten' were a ban on benefit, the Torah should have written 'one shall not benefit,' or at least just 'it shall not be eaten.' Why add 'its flesh'? To teach that even if he made it into kosher-style meat by slaughtering it, it is still forbidden.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא defends the ברייתא's reading. It shows that 'לא יאכל את בשרו' is about a slaughtered ox and not a ban on benefit.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבי אבהו's rule is limited to cases where 'לא יאכל' is the source of the eating ban. By the ox, stoning already makes it forbidden to eat, so these words are not needed for eating at all. The word 'בשרו' (its meat) points to an ox that became real meat through שחיטה, and it tells us that this ox is still forbidden.

steps.confusionAlert: The answer does not reject רבי אבהו's rule. It only says the rule does not fit here, because the ox's eating ban comes from somewhere else.
steps.whatToRemember: By the stoned ox: 'סקל יסקל' forbids eating it, 'את בשרו' forbids even a slaughtered ox, and 'בעל השור נקי' forbids benefit.
